newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Hungary, with '56 memory, yearns for NATO.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hungary, with '56 memory, yearns for NATO.

text.p: Hungary's fighter fleet is down to 50 MiGs, ageing Soviet-made equipment litters its bases and American-made bullets won't work in many Hungarian army rifles.
But this central European country, with a Soviet invasion in 1956 still a vivid memory, says it is eager to join and integrate into the NATO of the 21st century, and the sooner the better.
"We need the help of the Western countries, just like it was 50 years ago in the Marshall Plan," Lieutenant-General Ferenc Vegh, Hungary's top general, told Reuters.
His remark echoed a famous radio broadcast appealing to the world to "Help Hungary" after Soviet tanks invaded in November 1956, crushing Budapest's short-lived revolution.
With the collapse of communism in 1989, Hungary's military planners no longer look upon Russia as an immediate threat.

But they are clearly relieved that NATO and Russia are on track to sign a charter agreement in Paris this month, ahead of a July summit in Madrid where Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland are expected to be the first former East-bloc states to be asked to join NATO.
"It is not that there is any concrete threat from Russia," said Imre Mecs, head of parliament's defence committee and a 1956 veteran who spent six years in jail after the uprising.

"Still I believe central Europe belongs to the Western part of Europe and must join its security system," he said in an interview. "From the point of view of security, one must always prepare for the worst-case scenario."

If that worst case were to present itself today, however, Hungary would be hard-pressed to respond. The new member state that the 16-nation NATO alliance is contemplating admitting is anything but an up-to-date military power.
OUT WITH THE OLD
Over the past few years, Hungary has scrapped or disposed of outdated equipment, including more than half of its fleet of MiGs, but has had little or no money to buy replacements.

It is closing bases and has drastically reduced its army, which will number just 60,000 by year's end compared to 155,700 in 1989, in line with treaties signed after the collapse of communism to reduce conventional forces in Europe.
Hungary has instituted civilian control of the military, will cut conscription time to nine months from 12 in November and plans to have an all-professional army early next century.

Hungary has also been an enthusiastic participant in NATO's Partnership for Peace manoeuvres, designed to give former East bloc countries a taste of Western tactics, and provides bases for the NATO-led Bosnian peacekeeping operations.

But Hungary's defence budget this year was 97 billion forints, or about $570 million, just 1.4 to 1.5 percent of GDP and far less than defence analysts say it must spend to keep abreast of modern technology.

"We're looking for producers of security and not just consumers of security and it's going to be a tough case to sell that Hungary is a producer without spending more money," said Jeff Simon, an analyst from the National Defense University in Washington who specialises in central and eastern Europe.

Cost estimates for expanding NATO to bring in East European countries run from a low of $35 billion through 2009, according to a Clinton administration study, to a high of $100 billion to $120 billion suggested by the Congressional Budget Office.
NOT SPENDING ENOUGH
Vegh acknowledges that Hungary is not spending enough on its military, but said "money's a hard question".
"You know, we have had some difficulty with budgets in Hungary because during the last few years we cannot get enough money for the Hungarian army's requirements," he said.
"But I can tell you that NATO will not be a costly organisation, because defence is much cheaper within an alliance than outside the organisation."

Istvan Gyarmati, deputy state secretary of defence for integration, said that among politicians and administration officials he met in Washington recently, "everybody agreed that if NATO is enlarged Hungary should be one of the invitees".

He said meeting Hungary's military needs would be easier inside the framework of NATO, and said expected growth in Hungary's economy this year after several years of stagnation should cushion the blow domestically.
A Gallup Poll in March showing 47 percent of Hungarians want to join NATO, 27 percent oppose membership and 26 percent have no opinion indicates strong support, Gyarmati said.
LARGE MARGIN

"This is a very large margin which you would not necessarily find in all NATO countries," he said. "I have no doubt about the readiness and enthusiasm of Hungarians for NATO and EU membership because Hungarians consider our integration in these two organisations as part of the same process."

A big air show in the central city of Kecskemet near the end of May, and a "NATO Express" publicity train on which opinion makers, officials and journalists will discuss NATO-related topics, are all intended to win over the holdouts.
If NATO membership is offered in July, it will only mark the beginning of yet another long process of upgrading and reshaping the Hungarian army, but will be welcomed by many soldiers and officers.

Lieutenant-Colonel Jozsef Nyers, forced to move with his family from a base being closed in the southern city of Szeged to one 60 km (40 miles) away in Szentes, said he decided Hungary should join NATO when he worked alongside Italian NATO troops rebuilding railway lines in Bosnia.
"I was impressed by the attitude of the soldiers and because they were hard-working and disciplined," Nyers said in an almost barren office at his new base.
"The NATO troops are very self-confident. This is important in an army and this is what we need in the Hungarian army."
